opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, because we really do use AI heavily in our day-to-day work. For things like writing small patches, explaining unfamiliar code, or drafting tests, it's already very helpful. But fully automating maintenance of a project like vLLM is a different story, and I'd point to a few reasons.

First, vLLM sits at an awkward intersection of many layers. There's the model side, with new architectures coming out almost every week. There's the hardware side: different GPUs, different accelerators, each with its own kernels and quirks. And in between there's the scheduling logic, memory management, distributed execution, and so on. A lot of the hard bugs aren't inside one file. They come from how these layers interact, sometimes only on a specific hardware configuration, at a specific batch size, under a specific load pattern. To debug that, you often need to actually run things on real machines, look at performance traces, and form a hypothesis based on experience. Current AI tools aren't great at that kind of long, messy, empirical loop yet.

Second, much of maintenance isn't really about code. It's about judgment. When someone opens a PR, the question usually isn't "does this compile" or even "is this correct." It's "should this be in vLLM at all?" Does it add complexity that will hurt us in six months? Does it conflict with the direction we're heading in the core architecture? Is this contributor going to stick around and maintain the feature? Those decisions depend on context that mostly lives in people's heads: past discussions, design trade-offs we've already made, conversations with hardware vendors and model teams. It isn't written down anywhere an AI could read.

Third, there's the community side. vLLM is an open-source project with a huge number of contributors from many companies, and they have different interests. Part of maintenance is coordination: negotiating priorities, keeping people motivated, resolving disagreements politely. That's fundamentally human work built on trust.

And finally, the cost of mistakes is high. Many companies run vLLM in production. A subtle regression in performance or numerical correctness might not show up in CI but could affect a lot of users. So we need someone who is ultimately accountable, who understands why a change was made and can stand behind it.

So my view is that AI makes each maintainer much more productive, and that share will keep growing. But the "maintainer" role, meaning taste, direction, and responsibility, isn't something we can hand off yet. Maybe someday, but not today.

r001.rationale: It says key design trade-offs and project context live in maintainers’ heads, including past discussions and conversations with vendors and model teams.

r002.rationale: It mentions whether a PR’s complexity may hurt in six months and whether it fits the project’s direction, but does not clearly state that maintenance must anticipate future requirements rather than just address current problems.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that most of the hard work in maintaining vLLM isn't really the kind of work that AI is good at yet. People imagine maintenance as "a bug comes in, someone reads the traceback, writes a patch." That part, sure, models are getting quite good at. If you give an agent a clean reproduction and a clear failing test, it can often find the fix faster than I can.

But that's maybe ten or twenty percent of what we actually do. The rest is deciding what should happen, not how to make it happen.

Take a typical day. A new model architecture drops, and three different people open PRs to support it. One of them hacks it into the existing attention path, one adds a new backend, one changes the scheduler. All three "work" in the sense that the tests pass. The real job is figuring out which direction keeps the codebase coherent six months from now, when there are five more architectures like this one. That requires knowing the history: why we rejected a similar abstraction last year, which hardware vendors are depending on an interface we'd be touching, who on the team has context to review the result. An AI agent reading the repository sees the code, but it doesn't see the arguments we had in Slack, or the constraints that come from NVIDIA and AMD and Google all shipping on the same code path.

The second thing is that the ground truth is physical. vLLM runs on real GPUs, with real kernels, real NCCL versions, real driver quirks. A lot of the issues we get are "it works on H100 but hangs on MI300" or "throughput dropped three percent after this commit on this specific configuration." You can't reason your way to those answers from the source code. You have to run it, on hardware that is expensive and scarce, and then interpret noisy numbers. Models today are weak at exactly that part: knowing when a measurement is noise versus a regression, and knowing when the cheapest experiment is to just ask the person who wrote the kernel.

Third, and this is the part people underestimate, open source maintenance is social. A huge amount of the work is reviewing other people's contributions and giving feedback in a way that keeps them contributing. It's negotiating with companies that want their feature merged yesterday. It's saying no gracefully. When someone from a startup sends a 4000-line PR, the right response is usually not a fix, it's a conversation about splitting it up and about whether the project wants to own that code at all. I don't want a bot making those calls on behalf of the community, and I don't think contributors would accept it either.

Now, I do use these tools a lot, and the trajectory is clear. Triage, first-pass review, writing tests, bisecting regressions, porting a kernel from one backend to another: all of that is increasingly delegated. What's left for humans is converging on taste and responsibility. Someone has to be accountable when a release breaks production for people serving models at scale. Right now that someone has a name and a GitHub handle, and I think that's actually important for trust.

So my short version is: the parts of maintenance that look like coding are being automated quickly. The parts that look like judgment, under hardware constraints, with a community attached, are not. And those turn out to be the parts that keep the project alive.

r001.rationale: The response says maintainers need project history and context, including why past abstractions were rejected and which vendors depend on affected interfaces—context an agent may not see.

r002.rationale: It describes choosing an architecture approach that will keep the codebase coherent six months later, anticipating five more architectures rather than addressing only the current one.

astra-6.text:
I think AI can help with a lot of the work, but maintenance is more than writing a patch. You have to decide whether a reported issue is a real bug, understand the conditions that trigger it, and judge whether a fix will create problems elsewhere. For something like vLLM, correctness and performance both matter, and behavior can depend on the model, the hardware, and the workload.

An AI can propose a change, but how do we know that change is good? Passing the existing tests is useful, but the tests don’t capture every situation. You may need to reproduce the issue on particular hardware or measure performance under a particular workload.

So I see AI as a useful assistant to maintainers. The part that’s still hard to automate is closing that loop: understanding the problem, getting convincing evidence, and taking responsibility for the decision to merge.

r001.rationale: The response discusses understanding issues, test limits, and maintainer responsibility, but does not identify maintainers’ accumulated project context as a barrier.

r002.rationale: The response focuses on diagnosing and validating current issues; it does not say maintenance must anticipate future requirements.

sol-6.1.text:
I think AI can help a lot with individual tasks, but maintaining vLLM is more than writing code. You have to understand what a change means for correctness, performance, and compatibility across different models and hardware. A patch can look perfectly reasonable and pass the existing tests, yet cause a regression in a workload those tests don’t cover.

The harder part is deciding what should change and what evidence is enough to merge it. If someone reports a performance problem, is it a bug, a configuration issue, or a tradeoff we intentionally made? AI can help investigate, but a maintainer still needs to frame the problem, evaluate the evidence, and take responsibility for the decision.

So I see automation expanding as we improve testing and make performance easier to measure. But generating a patch and knowing that it’s safe to ship are still two different things.

r001.rationale: The response says maintainers must understand correctness, performance, and compatibility and evaluate evidence, but it does not identify their accumulated project context as a barrier.

r002.rationale: The response discusses investigating current problems and deciding whether patches are safe to ship, but does not say maintenance must anticipate future requirements.
